extracted.intended_audience: patent lawyers, judges, law students, and practitioners advising on Canadian patent obviousness
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for applying legal tests of obviousness in Canadian (and comparative U.K.) patent law, focusing on the role of experimentation, predictability, and the attributes of the hypothetical skilled person.

rubrics_metrics.name: If trial and error are required, it can’t be obvious
rubrics_metrics.description: “Trial and error” suggests that research or experimentation has an unexpected, unsuccessful component. The “error” portion suggests that the skilled worker is going in the wrong direction, learning what didn’t work rather than going in the plain and 'obvious' direction of what would be expected to be a successful result. Thus anything that requires 'trial and error' cannot be obvious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trial and error indicates an unpredictable research path with intermediate failures and dead ends, not a route that leads 'directly and without difficulty' to the solution. Examples: unpredictable properties of separated isomers or unexpected beneficial properties of specific salts (e.g., bisulfate salt). If the skilled person would have to pursue such trial-and-error work, the claimed invention is not obvious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experiments with unpredictable results indicate non-obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: When you cannot predict the result of an experiment before you run it, the result is not obvious. In some experiments the result is an unanticipated outcome and a 'Eureka' moment; for such results a patent is usually available, subject to other invention criteria.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish exploratory research (unpredictable outcomes) from confirmatory testing. Research typically uses current scientific knowledge to guide attempts, but if one does not know ahead of time whether success will be found or in what form, that unpredictability supports non-obviousness. Conversely, if the experiment's result is highly predictable (confirmatory rather than exploratory), the result is obvious.

rubrics_metrics.name: If research was needed, the invention was not obvious
rubrics_metrics.description: Legal articulation: for something to be 'obvious' it must be something that would directly occur to someone searching for something novel without the necessity of his having to do any experimenting or research (whether in the laboratory or amongst literature).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited authorities: Osram Lamp Works v. Pope; J.R. Short Milling; H.G. Fox treatise. The test requires that the notional skilled person would arrive at the invention without experimenting or serious thought. Experiments where results were not 'sufficiently predictable' (i.e., true research) indicate the invention lies outside the obvious path and so is inventive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Would, not could — 'very plain' test (no inquiries/testing for the hypothetical skilled person)
rubrics_metrics.description: The relevant test is not whether anyone skilled could have achieved the same result (i.e., 'could') but whether the result would have been 'very plain' (i.e., 'would') to the unimaginative technician. The hypothetical skilled person must find the invention 'very plain' without making inquiries, testing, or research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lederman J.'s 'Would, not Could' formulation (Bayer v. Apotex) rejects assessing obviousness by whether the skilled person could have reached the invention by testing. The mythical Canadian skilled technician cannot be credited with inquiring or thinking that ultimately leads to the answer; he/she must instantly and spontaneously see the answer. This distinguishes Canadian approach from some U.K. approaches that allow 'worth a try' reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree of experimentation required — undue experimentation renders discovery non-obvious
rubrics_metrics.description: If the invention requires undue experimentation (beyond routine, predictable testing), that fact renders the discovery non-obvious; routine or confirmatory workshop tests that are predictable do not support non-obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court distinctions: routine 'basic trial and error testing' or 'routine workshop activity' may be treated as non- inventive, whereas experimentation that is exploratory, unpredictable or constitutes undue experimentation supports a finding of non-obviousness. Assess whether steps could be overcome by 'pertinacity, sound technique or trial and error' alone or whether a 'spark of imagination' beyond ordinary skill is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: U.K. 'Worth a try' (obvious-to-try) test
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the traditional U.K. 'worth a try' test: 'It is enough that the person versed in the art would assess the likelihood of success as sufficient to warrant actual trial.' If chances of success are sufficient to warrant a trial, the matter is obvious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This test imposes a low bar for obviousness (if something is 'well worth trying' it may be obvious). Cases: Johns-Manville, General Tire, Technograph. The textbook cautions that the 'worth a try' test produced many UK patents held obvious and must be treated with care; it is not the Canadian test and was explicitly rejected in Canadian jurisprudence (see Bayer v. Apotex discussion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cripps question — 'for all practical purposes obvious' formulation
rubrics_metrics.description: The Cripps question asks whether it was, for all practical purposes, obvious to any skilled person in the state of knowledge existing at the date of the invention that the claimed result could be achieved (paraphrase used in Hoescht).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This pragmatic formulation focuses on whether the literature and general knowledge would have led the skilled chemist to conclude it was plain the process/product could be produced. It has been used historically in cases to frame whether a patent is valid; test requires examining the state of the art and the ordinary skilled person's practical expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper characterization/attribution of the hypothetical skilled person and research team
rubrics_metrics.description: When assessing obviousness, courts must correctly characterize the hypothetical skilled person (or members of a research team) and attribute the appropriate level of skill and problem‑solving ability to them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comparative case law (Mustill in Genentech vs Wetston) shows divergence: some authorities credit a skilled person with problem‑solving ability and the capacity to try reasonable routes, while Canadian cases (Lederman, Supreme Court) limit the notional person's capacity for inquiry/research. When an invention arises from collaborative research, the contribution of each notional team member should be assessed separately, attributing to each the requisite level of skill for their function.
